new_statements.quote: 12.2.4 Suprasegmental features. Accent, which only is contrastive in the verbal morphology, is realized as a high pitch: (3) ʕuki 'I/he drank' vs. ʕukí 'I/he do/does not drink'. Phonological accent induces the gemination of the following consonant: (4) ʔí=teeh-ti (INDV=give-PFV.3F) → [ʔítteːħti] 'she gave'. Any declarative utterance terminates with a final lowering in intensity. Instead, polar questions are marked by a final rise in pitch, accompanied by lengthening of the final vowel. When not coupled with suffixes, accentual modification of a stem is marked by the backslash (\).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Gawwada has a high-pitch accent, not dynamic stress. Its position is not fixed by syllable count: it is contrastive only in verbal morphology, where certain paradigms (negative imperfective, singular sequential) carry a final accent on the suffix, contrasting with segmentally identical affirmative perfective forms (ʕuki vs. ʕukí; ʕuk-ti vs. ʕuk-tí). Elsewhere accent is not marked; Tosco 2021 (p. 75, via Treis) says words 'may bear a lexical accent' but the prosody of unmarked words is not described. Black 1976 (p. 224) had earlier called Werizoid/Gawwada accent 'phonologically unpredictable'. Reading = pitch accent with morphologically (grammatically) determined placement; 'morphologically determined' is the alternative label since placement is a property of the affix/paradigm.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is otherwise triggered by specific morphology: the deictic form of nouns raises the final vowel 'which further attracts the accent' (-o → -ú, -e → -í, e.g. šaamɓ-ú 'this boy'); the 3rd-person subject clitic ʔí= is accented and geminates the following consonant; polar questions add a final pitch rise + vowel lengthening.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (verb forms and nouns in isolation), with a separate statement on utterance-final intonation (declarative lowering vs. interrogative rise). Concerns the dialect of Gawwada town and neighbouring villages (Western Dullay), not the Eastern Dullay dialects (Harso, Dobase, Gollango) grouped under ISO gwd.
new_statements.identity_note: Tosco 2023 (and his 2021 grammar) describe the dialect of Gawwada town and its neighbouring villages, a Western Dullay variety; ISO gwd / glottocode gaww1239 also subsumes the Eastern Dullay dialects Harso, Dobase, Gollango (which Amborn, Minker & Sasse 1980 describe) and Ale/Gobeze. Black 1976 'Werizoid' generalises across all Dullay varieties with Gawwada (Dalpeena village) examples. Ts'amakko (tsam1247) is the other Western Dullay language, described separately.

sources.note: §12.2.4 Suprasegmental features: accent is contrastive only in verbal morphology and is realized as a high pitch (ʕuki 'I/he drank' vs. ʕukí 'I/he do/does not drink'); phonological accent geminates the following consonant; declaratives end with lowered intensity, polar questions with a final pitch rise + lengthening. §12.8.1.2/12.8.1.4: negative-imperfective and singular sequential suffixes carry a final accent; §12.7.1: the deictic form raises the final vowel, which attracts the accent. No default placement rule for nouns/unmarked words is given.

sources.note: Second-hand on Tosco 2021: 'The section on the accent system consists of a mere four sentences (p. 70-71) and mentions accentual minimal pairs in the verbal system. As later elaborated on (§7, p. 210), the negative imperfective and the affirmative perfective are exclusively distinguished by accent, e.g. ʕuk-tí.. vs. ʕuk-ti'; only elements with an accentual opposition are marked with an acute; 'The prosodic realization of words transcribed without acute accents is not commented on, even though, as Tosco later mentions in passing (p. 75), "words may bear a lexical accent".'

sources.note: p. 224: 'Accent is phonologically unpredictable and is marked acute to the extent it has been recorded.' Covers all 'Werizoid' (Dullay) varieties, examples mostly Gawwada of Dalpeena.
